utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Usher, Mr. Usher, one preliminary matter -- let me first invite Madam Registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We all see what happens if you want to go too fast. The Defence announced that there was a preliminary matter to be raised. Or it was the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's very brief, Mr. President. And so the witness could probably be brought in while I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have a short matter to deal with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Prosecution has received the B/C/S translation for P6607, MFI, that's 65 ter 30856.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was exactly the same matter as I had. So the witness can be brought into the courtroom. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Unless you'd rather, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You started, so it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID R014-7186 B/C/S, and the Prosecution would request that this translation be attached and the document admitted into evidence. It was used with Witness Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber hereby requests the Registry to attach doc ID R014-7186 B/C/S to Exhibit P6607 and P6607 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, any -- anything for the Chamber to expect in relation to the video that was shown yesterday or -- there was a disclosure issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't intend to use the video. Regarding the video itself, we haven't reviewed fully what people are saying during the course of the video yet. As a result, I'd reserve the right to tender additional excerpts later for context, if necessary. I will be asking some questions about that incident this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But not using the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the matters that came to my mind is when I looked at the video and when I heard the sound, I wondered whether the sound was already there with the video, because it seemed not to, especially the explosions and what sounds of small arms fire. Of course, the last you can't verify but the first, it seemed not to correspond fully. I don't know where the sound comes from and whether it's original, "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave that to the parties for the time being. Good morning, Mr. Rasevic. Before we continue, I would like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to return now to the topic of civilians in Sedrenik and pick up from one of your answers yesterday. At transcript page 23612, you were asked: "And what you were concerned about happened, didn't it? VRS forces did fire at and hit civilians in Sedrenik." And you answered: "While I was with the company at Mrkovici, such things did not happen. Not once at least that I know of. Later on, I did hear that a girl was wounded or killed. I don't know what. But I'm terribly sorry. I'm sorry for the life of every child or person. But I really don't know anything about that as I wasn't there at the time." Do I understand that your evidence is that the girl who was wounded or killed was shot after you left the 3rd Company at Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At that time, I wasn't there and I cannot say anything about that incident or that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 13730? And this will be a United Nations weekly summary dated 18 to 24 June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's during the time that you were at Spicasta Stijena, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes, I was still commander of the Mrkovici company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand there is a released B/C/S version in the system but we have two Englishes on our screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In e-court we have a -- yes. We now have the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So looking at 20 June -- the third point, 20 June, and the first subpoint below it is: "1 x BiH civilian killed by SA fire, Sedrenik area." So this document is reporting that a civilian in the Sedrenik area was hit and killed by VRS fire, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'd put to you that civilians in Sedrenik were also hit by VRS fire during your time in the company.

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed about this case. I heard about this later through the media. Whether that civilian was killed by VRS fire, it could reasonably have been killed by the Muslim forces. At that time it was much easier to hit from their positions rather than from Spicasta Stijena because there was a great difference in elevation. So I cannot say whether it was or was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, if you don't know, fine. But then to explain how likely it is that the others did it and not your troops is speculation, is opinion, and is not knowledge about facts. If you say the report doesn't say -- doesn't give any details, that, again, I think that's fair to say, but then to start speculating how much easier it was for the one party than for the other party is just speculation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 13730 receives number P6642, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. In view of the comment of the witness, Mr. Traldi, is there -- are there any further details available on this incident which we only see here in a summary, weekly summary. Are there any other reports which shed more light on the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We could look into it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Moloto has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, you say you heard about this incident from the media. What actually did you hear? Did it report that a BiH civilian was killed by fire from the VRS? Well, what did -- what did the report say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's exactly how it was. At the time the Muslim or BiH media reported on a daily basis on many casualties, among others, about this, that by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Forget about the other incidents. I'm talking about this incident only. Was it reported that it was done by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly how they reported, the BiH media, TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As commander, did you then try to investigate, to find the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, I walked the defence line, I discussed and interviewed my men asking whether any of them did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the result of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Result was that nobody fired at civilians, that there was a skirmish between the trenches, Borovi [phoen] III, and another trench up there in the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you have a military written report about the incident from those you inquired from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't it procedure that when matters are investigated they are recorded in writing and reported to the commands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I reported to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, in writing. Do you have a report in written form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I reported in writing. I kept a log, but what happened with that, I don't know. After I left, I jotted down every incident, every skirmish, every exchange of fire, I reported in writing to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you talked about this incident you seemed to be surprised to hear of this kind of incident. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. You're not erring in this. There were incidents but there was no direct fire aimed at civilians. If you allow me, how to put it, we did not prevent the civilians from cutting down trees because for firewood. I did not prevent them in that. If in such a case there were -- there was an exchange of fire, it could have been possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just hold it there. Let me quote to you what you said yesterday, which was quoted to you just this morning. You said: "While I was with the company at Mrkovici, such things did not happen." So according to you, this kind of incident didn't happen while you were there. And then you say: "Not once, at least that I know of. Later on, I did hear that a girl was wounded or killed." This does not accord with what you have just told us, that you did investigate this incident. Do you agree with that? You couldn't have investigated if it didn't happen in your time. One of the two cannot be correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked the men, the fighters, asked them, "Did you by any chance fire at civilians?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the response was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "Well, there was a skirmish" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. If you did investigate any such incident, you wouldn't say nothing of the sort happened during our time. Is it not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in response to one of Judge Moloto's questions he asked about incidents where civilians were hit by sniper fire and you said there were incidents. About how many were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim or state about those. I heard about this case concerning this girl. I don't know whether it was true. I heard about it. And this case that we discussed just a minute ago. But how this incident happened, this is something I cannot state with any clarity or certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then, sir, I want to return to the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we get an answer to the question of Mr. Traldi? You explained to us that you do not know the details, but the question was when you said that these incidents happened, how many you are aware of. One? Two? Ten? 20? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean incidents at Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to my knowledge, serious attacks numbered ten-odd. Every day, exchange of fire was common. There would be a rifle, grenades coming from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, again we are talking about civilians being hit by fire from Spicasta Stijena. We are talking about incidents, not about combat. How many of such incidents you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about this case that we discussed, that a civilian was wounded. How, I don't know. And I heard about this case concerning the girl. I just heard it later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So altogether, two? Or is it one because it -- I'm not aware that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one that I know of. I do not know about this other incident about which I only heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, although you told us that through the media that you learned that you were blamed again and again for this kind of incidents. Isn't this what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you, during the day I did not know that this incident had happened. Only in the evening, once I heard news on the media, I heard that one man had been wounded. Initially I heard he was wounded, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You are constantly giving answers to questions that are not put to you. You told us that you were blamed again and again in the media about this type of incidents, and you said you only learned about these one or two, I leave that alone, cases. If that's your evidence, fine, then -- but I just put it to you that you told us a minute ago that you were frequently blamed for -- in the media for this type of incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they blamed us throughout the war that we attacked relentlessly which does not correspond to the truth, and this is what I said, this is the context in which I said that. I'm not just talking about this particular incident but throughout the war they blamed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So just to make sure I understand your last answer, you regularly read reports that civilians had been injured by fire from Spicasta Stijena and other locations, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read reports. I just heard about it in the media. Serbian television, Bosnia-Herzegovina television, and other televisions available to me. I'm not going to say never, but there were very few days when they did not report that Mrkovici killed and maimed and wounded this or that many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I renew my request to tender the document. The witness has heard about this specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it may have been given a number but not formally admitted yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document has been assigned number P6642, I would just [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, to conclude, I want to return to the video Mr. Stojanovic showed you. I'm not going to show it again, but I want to summarise your evidence to make sure we have it clear. Do you recall the video?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the time the video began, you were 200 metres behind the front line in your company's command, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You couldn't see what was happening at the beginning of the video, but once the explosions started you ran outside and you could see; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The ABiH soldiers who were attacking Spicasta Stijena were part of a unit called Black Swans or "Crni Labudovi"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The ABiH held the position only overnight, they did not advance any further, and you took it back the next morning. That's correct too, right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And one trench was blown up completely, right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30939? This is a daily combat report from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 19 September 1994. And, Your Honours, it's only partially translated. We located it over night, but the part I'm interested in is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Defence is able to read the remainder of the document -- Mr. Stojanovic, if you consider there to be important information for the Chamber, then you should ask for a translation of the whole of the document because I see on the non-translated part already reference to Grdonj and Spicasta Stijena, so I'm not saying that that is relevant but I see those names already under item 1, aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're happy to put in a request, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But if we look at point 2, labelled "Our Forces," it says in pertinent part: "At Sarajevo battlefield, on the day of 18/9/1994, have been executing combat actions in order to occupy Spicasta Stijena and Mala Kula. For these tasks, forces were engaged comprising one platoon from the 120th BBR, Crni Labudovi," and then it lists some other units. Where we read Crni Labudovi, that's the Black Swans unit you identified in the video, right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Beginning of the next paragraph reads: "Upon commencement of action, 120 BBR," and again that was identified above as that Black Swans unit, "have captured a part of Spicasta Stijena." That's what you testified happened in the video you were describing, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It next says: "The unit PTDO MUP Bosna had executed the attack right of Spicasta Stijena and the same have, upon commencement of attack, destroyed one trench." Your testimony is that the destruction of a trench happened in the incident you saw and it was fortified more strongly afterwards, right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And looking at the bottom of the page, it says -- well, immediately afterwards, it says: "By the nightfall units occupied Spicasta Stijena." And it's right that the ABiH occupied Spicasta Stijena overnight on that one occasion, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, part of Spicasta Stijena. Part was not -- it was not -- the Spicasta Stijena was not completely under their control but just that part where this trench that had been hit was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'd put to you that this is the incident that you described yesterday and the report clearly dates it as having happened on the 18th of September 1994. I'd put to you that you are mistaken about the date, and the incident you described is the same as the one Mr. Gengo testified about, the one described in this report, and occurred in September of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters do not know what exactly your answer is, Witness. Could you tell us whether you agree with Mr. Traldi that you may be mistaken as far as the date is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite possible because I don't have the date itself in any of my notes. That was something that was left behind at the company when I left. It's quite possible that it happened then, at the time when Gengo said it happened and the time where it is reported that we see here, because this was a report to the battalion commander, so I can then confirm that that's how it was. Because for some other reasons, thinking of when Sinisa and I took turns, at the command in August, he -- it was his wedding, and then -- so I was trying to figure out based on that, but it's quite possible seeing what it says here that it was at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, your testimony was that you were at the company command when that happened but it sounds like your evidence is you'd become Mr. Gengo's deputy in the battalion command at that point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. However, very frequently, as the Mrkovici Company was vulnerable in that section where it suffered the greatest number of attacks, I was there a lot of the time, and we also had a forward command post there, a battalion forward command post, and I spent a lot of time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm reminded that I've neglected to tender the document 30939. I'd ask that it be marked for identification until we've got a complete translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30939 receives number P6643, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, just a few. Could we have in e-court P6641, page 2 of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for it to come up, let me just say that it's a document used by the Prosecution from the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade dated the 29th, 1992, and I would like to refer you to item 4, Mr. Rasevic. Yesterday you were referred to this part, and especially the part where it says: "I have decided by applying various offensive combat actions, extend the attack along the following axis: Krusevo village, Dolovi village, Olovo and Ponijerak village..." And then if I'm reading this correctly: "Donji Drecelj village, Paklenik, Grabovica village." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Where is Olovo in relation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Olovo is to the north-west of Sarajevo, some 50 to 60 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the villages of Krusevo, Dolovi, and Ponijerak are?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know the main highway, Sarajevo-Olovo and so on, but I have heard of Krusevo because I have a lot of neighbours who were from that area, but I don't know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Krusevo village from vary?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Krusevo is also about 60 kilometres, like Olovo, perhaps a kilometre or two closer or further, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question is this: When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue there, you read to the witness at least that's how it is on the record, Grabovica village. Now, the English version says Grahovica with an H rather than with a B, and looking at the original I think it's not perfectly clear whether it's an H or whether it's a B. But I just wanted to put on the record that what you are recorded to have read is not consistent with the English translation of a rather unclear B/C/S original. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I would like to ask you, Mr. Rasevic: While you were in the Mrkovici Company, were there several attacks on Spicasta Stijena and were there several times when Spicasta Stijena was captured by the BH Army for brief periods at least?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There were several attacks and there was some capturing, once or twice, but that would last for an hour or two. So it was only on that one night that they actually held it, the entire night. But what usually happened is they would start shooting or a shell would fall, then these men would withdraw and then I would return there and someone with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your positions, and I mean the fortifications, trenches and communication trenches, did they run along the ridge, the ridges Krs I Krs II, Krs III of the Spicasta Stijena feature or were they placed differently?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were a bit closer to our position because had they been on the very lip of the ridge, it would have been -- they would have been far easier targets. However, they were a bit withdrawn from there and, yes, we had these communication trenches and reserve communication trenches, reserve trenches and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These trenches, were they dug out or were they built up, constructed features?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the trenches were dug in and where it was impossible to dig them in because of the ground that was rock, then we would construct some kind of screen. There would be construction. A lot of stones or rocks would be piled up, one on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will conclude with another question about this. In terms of the time of this incident, what were you guided by when you determined what time this happened? What was -- what were your considerations? What were you -- what was your meaning?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a takeover between me -- well, the takeover of duties between me and Sinisa Maksimovic as commanders of this company. I know this took a couple of days. So I thought that this happened before he got married. Now, I mention his wedding again. But most probably, as I don't have the date noted down, it happened as Gengo said, on the 18th of September because these reports were sent to the command. So that's how it must have been. That's all that I was guided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember whether during this operation that was filmed on that video, on that occasion was the position of your unit also captured, the Mala Kula feature?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not at that time. Mala Kula was captured on the 29th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also spoke about this in your statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rasevic, thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, there's one issue which I'd like to have perfectly clear. That's the reason why I revisit it because Mr. Stojanovic did so as well. Yesterday, we looked at this video. We saw soldiers moving mainly on the left side of the screen, and more on the right side of the screen we saw at certain points in time explosions, flashes. You could see the light of that. Could you tell us where we saw that light, these explosions, were these your fortifications or trenches, whatever you call them?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Flashes could be clearly seen when they struck our trench, the trench that they destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could clearly see them. I didn't ask whether we could clearly see them. But what we saw, those flashes, those flashes were in the location where your trenches were?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Other than these, these were below our trenches, below our trenches, and then if we were to see this again, we would see that all these three trenches at Spicasta Stijena were attacked at the same time. Here they were only filming the one that was being captured, whereas all the three were being attacked, the one on the right which was called Krs I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I want to see it again. Could we play that video again, especially the -- I think it was the first of the two videos, there were two portions, and is it possible to play it again. And when I say "stop," could we then stop the movement. I'm sorry for not having the number available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the record, I think it's D553, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see Mr. Ivetic is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to get the computer to co-operate with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- applying --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It will take about a minute or two to get the computer up and running for the video to be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the 65 ter number, if that would be helpful for Mr. Ivetic, is 1D2992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps meanwhile I ask a question. Did you find this video yourself on the internet, Witness?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some friends of mine who saw it told me about it. It's been a while already, maybe some ten years or so, that it's been on YouTube.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties verified in any way whether this appears on YouTube and from what sources or?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can say I've verified that it appears on YouTube, but that's the extent of the verification I've been able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That sounds -- that's either the start-up or the very end. There we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we stop already here, right away. Witness, what you see on your screen now, we see the -- what seems to be two rocky formations, one a little bit more to the left, one a little bit further back to the right. Can you describe where your fortifications can be seen here?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, our fortification, our trench, was on the right-hand side. It's a bit in the back of this peak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that approximately at the location where the tree with most green is located? There's one tree which apparently is more green than the other ones. Is that approximately --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly where it is. Not approximately but precisely there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And right of it we can see some dried up trees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who is controlling the mouse. Could you try to follow the one -- I see there the tree with the most, you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you then guide the person who is controlling the mouse to where your trenches were. Is it further down? Is it --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lower down, at the base of the tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is that --

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Behind the tree?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the tree, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we see is still what looks a bit like a rocky formation with a few black spots. Is that approximately where your fortification can be seen? Where the mouse is now? Where the pointer is now?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the so-called Krs III peak of Spicasta Stijena. That's what it's called. And it is practically in the rock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was this a kind of a built-up trench or fortification or was it a dug-in trench or fortification?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dug-in trench from this other side, from our side. There is a high rock there and we built the trench into this rock, and there were also firing openings there, and we covered it and so on. So this was a reconnaissance trench, an observation trench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you make fire openings in that same trench?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The so-called fire slits. There would be no trench without it. You can't leave a trench without these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we move on with the video at this moment. What we saw at this moment was at 00.20. That's what we looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One stop. Could we go back for just two or three seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop when we saw the big flash. That last flash we saw, is that a flash which is approximately where your trenches were?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the trench we saw a minute ago and you said that was heavily damaged. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: BLASKO RASEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the trench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last portion was at 00.32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we saw the flash a split second before that. I have no further questions. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any further questions by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Not for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but perhaps we could then tender this document and remove the MFI indication if the Prosecution agrees, that's D553.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We would ask for a little bit of time to investigate the source, Mr. President. I understand the images have to be part of the record to understand what the witness was referring to, but in terms of the other content we may wish to make additional submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We leave it for the time being MFI'd, but the Prosecution will revisit the matter within the next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We will do our very best to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you're unable to do so, please come with a report why you aren't able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your evidence, Mr. Rasevic. You've answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I thank you for that. I thank you for coming to The Hague and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. May I take it that the Prosecution is -- the Defence is ready to call its next witness after the break, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. And that's Colonel Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will take the break and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I address the following matter. We had not received it. Then we got it. Now I do understand that the order has been changed since then again. And it's thanks to Madam Registrar that the Chamber knows about it. I do understand that she was informed this morning, but the Chamber staff was not informed about the newest change, and I am fearful for the day where even when the witness enters the courtroom, the Chamber would not know who it is who will be examined. Next time any change in the schedule should not only be communicated with the Prosecution and with the Registry but preferably also to Chamber staff. We still have to play a role in the proceedings here. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honour, I just wanted to raise with the Chamber before the witness comes in that the witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We hear you. Perhaps you're ear phones are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That the witness did previously receive a 90(E) admonishment and we do believe it is proper for this witness to receive one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It always depends on the questions that are put to him, and we have a standing practice that the Defence should be very alert on it. But we leave it in the hands of the Defence to start with, whether a 90(E) caution will be given, and if the Chamber itself sees any reason halfway, it can still do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the 90(E) was given in the Karadzic case. I do not anticipate that my questions will raise its need but I leave it to Your Honours to be diligent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll carefully follow the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I do have to add that I believe the revised witness schedule was sent to Chambers -- at least the e-mail that I received was copied to the Mladic case Chambers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's the case --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- as of 9.00 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course I have to apologise. Then my staff might expect a similar critical note. We will find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, sorry not to pay proper attention to you entering the courtroom. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragicevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Good day. Good day to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by calling up 65 ter number 1D0168. A hard copy of the same was provided to Prosecution counsel and then given to the usher. And if we could have that in front of the witness, it might assist in terms of the speed of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you just check whether the number is correctly recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I must have misspoken. It's 1D01618. And thank Your Honour for bringing that to my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have anything on the screen. That may be -- now it is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, first I would ask you to take a look at the first page and tell us if you recognise the signature on that first page.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you in fact give a written statement to the Defence team of General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And subsequent to signing this document, did you have occasion to review the same during proofing the other day in order to verify if there were any necessary corrections?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would at this time like to look at paragraph 2 which is to be found on page 2 in both versions of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, where in paragraph 2 you are recorded as saying: "Before the Drina Corps was established, we were not visited by anyone and we could not go anywhere." Is that accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct in its entirety, if we mean land communications or roads because all of them were not safe. It was not safe to move around, and very few dared take those roads. So whoever was supposed to come and visit us would do so very rarely. I remember that General Mladic, risking too much, visited my brigade once but he flew on a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to paragraph 10, which is to be found on page 4 of both versions of the document. And actually it will be -- the relevant part will be I think on page 5 of both documents. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where you are recorded as saying: "It is my belief that even now in 2002 the Sarajevo airport has no competence over air traffic in the BH air space."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think you misspoke. You said 2002 but I read 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 2012. Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any clarification you wish to make to this section of paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the clarification is this: I'm sure that as at 2012 Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have air traffic control, control of its air space, and I do believe that this still holds today but I'm not certain. So -- which means that they have not established control over air traffic -- control over air traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to take a look at paragraph 23, which is to be found on page 6 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph, you outline the various ABiH units which were present in the theatre of war where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was. Are all the ABiH units identified here or are there any forces missing?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: 31st Division of the ABiH with its headquarters at Gorazde is missing from this -- correction, 81st.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from these corrections and clarifications that we have now gone through, do you stand by everything that you have written in your statement as being accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I do believe this is accurate and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you questions today based on the material contained in your statement, would your answers be the same in substance as contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: In essence, these would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, would those answers to my questions be truthful as contained in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I will always speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I at this time move pursuant to Rule 92 ter to introduce 65 ter number 1D1618 into evidence along with the one associated exhibit, 65 ter number 1D02315.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That should be page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm that this is your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, do I understand that the objections raised in your response such as what kind of maps were used or -- that you do not further object? I remember an observation about I think it was paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Map showing deployment on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The -- we leave it to the Defence if they want to further explore it, but with respect to the content --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- of the statement we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assign numbers first to the statement, second to the associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Statement document 1D1618 receives number D554. And document 1D2315 receives number D555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D554 and D555 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time I would like to read a public summary of the witness statement. The procedure has been explained to the witness during proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Dragicevic was a lieutenant-colonel in the JNA airforce in 1992, when the war broke out, stationed at Rajlovac in Sarajevo. He joined the VRS in July of 1992, being first assigned as the Chief of Staff of the Visegrad Brigade and later brigade commander. In 1993, he was named chief of staff of the Visegrad tactical group and served until November 1994 at which time he was named the assistant commander for morale, for religious, and legal affairs in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Colonel Dragicevic's testimony covers harassment of JNA personnel in 1991 in Sarajevo by Juka Prazina and other persons that later became the embryo of the Muslim armed forces. He describes briefings in the JNA that told of Muslim and Croat personnel being trained by the BH Ministry of Interior and the ZNG, as well as a training centre of the Patriotic League established at Igman. Colonel Dragicevic states that not a single member of the JNA was dismissed from duty due to their ethnicity. Slovenes and Croats left first voluntarily and then Bosnian Muslims left en masse in March and April 1992, especially when it was clear the JNA would pull out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness recalls fire being opened at night on the JNA from Butmir settlement on the south side of the airport. Meetings with representatives of that settlement revealed that the Sandzaklije Muslims from Serbia were responsible, firing mortars mounted to vehicles. The witness also recalls attacks upon the withdrawing JNA by the SDA and the HDZ, such as the attack on the JNA army command in Sarajevo and the JNA columns withdrawing from Sarajevo and Tuzla. In the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the strategy was to defend the living space of the Serbian people and to protect itself and the other loyal citizens in the area of Sarajevo and Romanija. The ABiH outnumbered the SRK 3 times to 1. The SRK fired only on registered enemy firing positions that caused casualties among VRS soldiers or civilians. The SRK forbade action against UNPROFOR. The ABiH often fired upon the SRK from near UNPROFOR installations. Colonel Dragicevic does not know of a single case or war crime committed in the area of responsibility of the SRK during the time period that he was a member of the SRK command. He recalls that the Main Staff of the VRS asked for the Markale I incident to be investigated by a mixed military commission including VRS representatives but that this was refused by the Muslims as was the offer made by the Serb side for Sarajevo to be an open city. The witness states there was no siege to speak of in Sarajevo, especially when the ABiH constructed a tunnel under the airport. The SRK blockaded the ABiH 1st Corps and not the city itself. That concludes the public summary of the statement. With Your Honours leave, I would now have some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could first take a look at paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is to be found at pages 2 and 3 of both versions of the statement, and I'd like to focus on the last sentence in that paragraph which can be found on the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- here you mention being officially informed that a training centre of the Patriotic League was established at Igman. What was this league's affiliation?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Patriotic League was a military formation of the Party of Democratic Action or the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with another group known as the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was a police force of the SDA. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to paragraph 11 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is to be found on page 4 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here you talk about the so-called Sandzaklije shooting from Butmir on the JNA with mortars mounted on vehicles and that representatives of the settlement told you about this. Can you give us more information about who is the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: We held meetings with representatives of this sizeable, predominantly Muslim inhabited settlement, and we discussed with the local community representatives. I remember a prominent businessman, Celanovic. Mostly we met at his home and sometimes in the local community premises. The information about vehicle mounted mortars was provided by them to us. The goal of those talks was not open fire at one another, to avoid unnecessary loss of life. They were interested in that. However, when I noticed that they'd dug trenches facing towards the air control building and the landing strip, I asked them why have you dug your trenches facing us? Why don't you dig in trenches which would prevent those Sandzaklije from entering your settlement? They promised they would do so but never came through with that promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of these local representatives that you met with?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How often did this fire upon the JNA from the Butmir settlement occur?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Every evening. Every evening after sunset, they would start firing from that settlement at our positions. First of all, the building of air control and our units, which were deployed in the area of the Butmir or Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next I would like to turn to paragraph 15, which should be on the same page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you make mention that: "We did not trust the international community because of the role it played in the events in Dobrovoljacka Street." Can you please identify for us what events at Dobrovoljacka street you are speaking of?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I refer to the massacre committed by the military and police of the SDA, Patriotic League, and Green Berets respectively. They attacked the staff of the 2nd Army District command who, in agreement with representatives of the civilian authorities headed by President Izetbegovic and General Mackenzie's, were forming a line, about to abandon their erstwhile headquarters, the neighbourhood of Bistrik, because they could not survive any longer there because there were daily attacks at the command headquarters building and loss of life of soldiers. At that point, many people lost their lives on the trucks, without any combat posture on their side. Many were wounded. And more than 100 were held prisoner. There were some Muslims among them; specifically, there was a woman who was a civilian working at the headquarters and an officer. Maybe there were more, but I'm sure about one who was a Muslim who also lost his life there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could briefly tell us if there were any other factors or incidents that were the bases of your conclusion that the international community could not be trusted?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at this point in time, and this was a dominant event and none of us could accept and understand that such a criminal act would be committed, a massacre, a crime, without any reaction whatsoever on the part of those who were conducting or leading the negotiations of the two sides, in other words the UNPROFOR, and my private view, when I was in Sarajevo, and I observed these things, it was my impression that as soon as members of UNPROFOR arrived in Bosnia, in some part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the conflict would flare up there. So it was all of our view that UNPROFOR took the enemy side by virtue of the fact that absolutely no response whatsoever happened after this crime in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other specific incidents that you'd like to again just briefly make reference to as we are pressed for time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I had several occasions to actually conclude that we were correct in our conclusion. In fact I worked and I was appointed by the commander of the Main Staff to be the VRS representative in the Gorazde sector and to liaise with UNPROFOR and the enemy side on the issues of maintaining peace and other agreements, such as anti-sniping -- the anti-sniping agreement and so forth. And when the Serbian army was supposed to withdraw, and we had already withdrawn some one and a half kilometres, and that too was unusual that only one side would have to withdraw, however, we accepted that as a fact. And then a British brigade arrived, the personnel was rather young, and they were supposed to impose themselves between the two warring sides. I remember the commander's name, rather first name, his name was David. When he arrived for these talks, and of course he was supposed to talk with me because I was in charge of co-operation with them, he told me that they were neutral, that he was -- that he wanted to make sure that none of his soldiers was killed, and he asked me what our view was on that, and I said, "Well, there wouldn't be any problem as long as you kept neutral. As long as you're neutral, we will not pose any problems." We, the Serbs who were there in the Gorazde sector. He accepted that and on the next day he brought his men. I was at the head of the column. He was behind me and it seemed as if I was actually leading his army. This was some 50 metres away from our defence line. And at one point after some 100 metres or so, I turned around and I realised that all of his soldiers had their rifles pointed at our soldiers, and then I wondered, I asked him, "Well, what is this? What is going on? Aren't you abiding by our agreement? You promised you would be neutral." And then he said, "Well, you know, this is how we were briefed. You would eat young kids and you're very dangerous," and so on. Well, I said, "Sir, but we have an agreement and we are abiding by it." And then he said, "Well, we are not sure that our soldiers would be safe." And then I said, "Well, I am not going to lead an army where my soldiers would have -- watch me bringing in a foreign unit that was in a combat posture against them." Then I said -- then he said -- well, when I said that I would deploy them, then they actually put their rifles away and abandoned the combat posture. There were a lot of other examples like this. When I was at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I also had occasion to see where they took civilians, alleged civilians, they would take them across the runway, the airport runway, only so these men would then get armed and cross Igman. Another example would be the tunnel under the runway, and UNPROFOR was responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Ivetic to briefly make reference rather than to tell us for ages matters which apparently were feeding your lack of trust. I do understand that you profoundly mistrusted UNPROFOR. Could you just point at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not have a profound distrust. What happened was that they were the ones who actually made me feel this way because in the beginning they made as if they were neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say who caused you to have that mistrust but it appears from your words that, and as you just confirmed a second ago, that they made you feel this way. That's fine. But you talked about the tunnel, and crossing to Igman, three or four sentences to explain. Did you want to add anything which we found already in the statement; that is, that apparently you considered that the UNPROFOR was not neutral in letting ABiH soldiers in and out through the tunnel? Is that what you -- do you want to add anything to what is in your statement in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to say that as time went by, and especially when I was actually in a position to work with them directly, I arrived at the conclusion that my initial impression was correct. There were a number of instances that confirmed this conduct of theirs. As the war progressed, they were taking more and more the side of our enemy -- of our opponent, opposing side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another topic, paragraph 16 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is to be found at page 5 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What could you tell us about the manner in which the SRK passed along orders about adherence to the international laws of war down the ranks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various manners, and the responsible officers from the company commander level, battalion commander and their assistants for morale, battalion commanders and their assistants for morale, directly trained their soldiers, and we did this usually during periods of cease-fire or truces, more often than not it was in winter months, February or March, and we conducted training. But it was impossible to train all our soldiers, but the lower level commanders had the duty to convey to every single fighter the things they learned at their training courses. As for morale, the area of morale, I was the one who instructed them. As for the legal affairs, there was an assistant for legal matters. He was a lawyer. And in the various brigades, the assistants for morale, legal, and religious affairs, these people were also trained. There were lawyers or -- had the similar background. Now, it was impossible to do this training for the entire -- for all the troops because they were deployed in various areas. However, we prepared various booklets that were adapted to the level -- the education level of the simple soldiers, the privates, so that they would be able to actually understand what the purpose of these courses was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us, moving on to another area, what can you tell us as to any problems between the local, political leaders on the one hand and the VRS on the other hand, beginning first in your time period in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was actually the first time when I saw that those people who knew least about the military and about the war were the ones who most wanted to become commanders. So these political structures actually attempted, especially in the beginning, but less so as time went on, to put forward their proposals and insist on them without actually having any responsibility for their implementation. They -- some commanders would just do as they were asked, they did not oppose that, but I took a different position. I was very strict. They tried the same thing when they came to meet with me, these local political leaders, but then I explained that that would not hold, that when a commander issued his order that was his final word, and because of this lack of knowledge they believed and felt that they were our superiors, that they were above us in this crisis situation, the wartime conditions. So I had problems with these local leaders because they tried in various ways to stand up to me but I did not -- I did not allow them to interfere in my work and I did not get involved in what they did, and most of the commanders that I knew did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last question: What can you tell us about the same topic in relation to your time spent at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that as time went on, in the third year of the war already, the influence was not as strong. I assumed that these political circles understood that they shouldn't interfere in things that they knew nothing about. I believe that Commander Milosevic had an even more intelligent position, if I can put it that way. I did as I did, but his position was, you know, just let them talk, and do their talking, and we will do our job. So he didn't want to stand up to them directly. He didn't want to oppose them directly. As I sit here in retrospect I think it was probably a smarter, that position was probably smarter of his although it wasn't fully a military stance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for your answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find him to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, except these few phrases such as, "okay," "good morning," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Today, at temporary transcript page 26, you mentioned that General Mladic visited the Visegrad brigade and he flew there on a helicopter. Could you please tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in August 1992, and he exposed had himself to a tremendous risk. But that was the only way, the only quick way and safe way, travelling by helicopter. This is in parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, today if you could listen to my questions. I'll try to be very specific. We appreciate what you've already said. There is no need to repeat it. Where did he visit you? Just asking for the location.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: At the Visegrad Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That was located inside the town of Visegrad, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What settlement in Visegrad was that command located in?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, nowadays it's a neighbourhood of the town itself but - nowadays - but in the past it was a settlement right next to a town where there was an elementary school before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And what was the settlement called?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know for certain. I know that it's Vojvoda Putnika Street nowadays. That's what it's called. But I don't really know what it was called. It was on the right bank of the Drina River and it was part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today, at temporary transcript page 33, you stated that you were appointed by the commander of the Main Staff to be the VRS representative in the Gorazde sector and to liaise with UNPROFOR. Is it correct that General Mladic appointed you to this position?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: The order came from the Main Staff of the VRS, and I believe General Mladic himself, but I'm not quite certain. But it did come from the command of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for those clarifications, Colonel. I'd now like to turn to your statement in this case and I believe you have a copy of it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Court Officer could please call up Exhibit D554. If we could please go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel, today I'm going to start by going through your statement in general terms. I just want to make sure that I understand it. The cover page of your statement indicates that you were interviewed on four separate dates. Were you interviewed by both Mr. Sasa Lukic and Mr. Zorko on each of these days?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I believe that on one occasion both of them were there, and then the other three occasions they would alternate, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Which date were they both there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I believe on the first meeting we had, the first interview, they were together. But I'm not sure. I didn't really pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you're pointing at dates. Is there any specific reasons why the cover page in English doesn't contain dates and why the B/C/S version does?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I actually just noticed that, Your Honours. I don't know. I could be -- I think these may be the batches that were first -- well, actually, I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if I find out in a second, I'm a bit surprised that those responsible for drafting and translating this have not noticed it. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did these interviews take place?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade. I apologise, actually. I just noticed that this was in 2013. The first interview was in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Then were the other three after that in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was anyone else present during any of these interviews besides Mr. Lukic and Mr. Zorko?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: In Visegrad, there was a man present but he didn't take any part in it. It was Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then if we could please go to the next page of the statement in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm just going to go through the parts of the statement to make sure I understand how it's organised. The first two paragraphs of your statement relate to your military career, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through your entire 30 year military career, but I do have a few specific questions. First, could you tell us whether there was any period of time between 1972 and 2002 where you were not a member of the armed forces in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question? I'm not sure I understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll try to make it more simple. Between 1972 and 2002, were you always an active member of the military?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was an active member of the military throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the first paragraph, you indicate that you lived in Sarajevo until May 1992 in the Breka settlement, is it correct that this is located in the area of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is in Sarajevo, right above the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In May 1992, when did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I left Sarajevo on the 9th or 10th of May 1992. If you mean when I actually left for good from Sarajevo or do you mean the town of -- the city of Sarajevo and my home when I left my house? What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Maybe this will be clear from the next question I have. In reviewing your statement, there was only one period where I cannot work out where you were at and where you were assigned. This period was between mid-May and mid-July 1992. Could you please tell us where you were during that time period?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: This period. At this time, in this period, as I was an officer in Rajlovac, I was assigned to the Butmir airport to be the battalion commander. There was a military section of the airport. And I remained there until the 9th or the 10th of May 1992 as a member of the centre, whereas my training centre had already moved out of Rajlovac and left for Belgrade, Batajnica, and Sombor. So about ten of us officers from the training centre -- the airforce training centre in Rajlovac left Sarajevo and were assigned to a new training centre, a new location of the training centre which for more specifically meant that I went to be Zarkovo near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that we are approaching a break. It's actually a good moment for a break time, if that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's close to the time when we need the break. If this is a suitable moment, we will take the break now. Witness, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. We take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic, as far as updating Chamber and Chamber staff, this morning, at 3 minutes past 9.00, a message was sent to I would say everyone involved, including Chamber staff, about witness scheduling for the next two weeks. Seven minutes later, a new list of witnesses for this week was sent to Madam Registrar, but to Madam Registrar only, and she was kind enough to inform Chambers staff. I don't know when the Prosecution received this information about the change of witnesses this week because I think the main difference being that Mr. Kecmanovic and Mr. Sehovac were reversed in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can report I spoke with Ms. Bibles on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't know the precise -- I think Ms. Bibles was told orally and we received the list from Madam Registrar as well, which we are grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's a different matter to speak to Ms. Bibles or to inform what you said earlier today, to inform the Chamber staff in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is my understanding -- I thought we were talking about this list which was sent at 9.03 which is the e-mail that I referenced in my prior comments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- which was sent to Chamber but now I see we're talking about the -- this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was talking about this week and about a recent change. If that change would have been known already last Friday and discussed with Ms. Bibles, because the order of Mr. Sehovac and Mr. -- one of the other witnesses was reversed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, Kecmanovic. Then if that would have been known already on Friday and discussed with Ms. Bibles on Friday --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Saturday. Saturday, 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Saturday. Then the Chamber would have liked to be informed already not only today but even yesterday about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Weber, if you're ready you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Dragicevic, before the break, you mentioned that there was a new training centre near Belgrade in Zarkovo. Did volunteers from Serbia receive training at this location?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: It was the airforce and air defence training centre. Who was trained there were cadets who had been trained at Rajlovac but were transferred and resumed their schooling at the new location, Zarkovo, Sombor, but as per a summary curriculum because immediate threat of war had obtained. And for us in Sarajevo, the war had already started and that was the cause for us transferring there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How long were you stationed at this training centre?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: You mean me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I was -- stayed there from the 10th or 11th May 1992 until my departure to Visegrad, to the VRS. In the meantime, since I attended command staff academy at the time, I used that period, I was invited, to attend command staff academy courses. That took part at Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
